newsitem.title: FINLAND: ASKO CEO SAYS GROUP STRUCTURE NOT COMPLETE.
newsitem.headline: ASKO CEO SAYS GROUP STRUCTURE NOT COMPLETE.

text.p: Even after a stream of divestments last year, Finnish plastic pipe goods, white goods and furniture maker Asko Oy will continue restructuring through asset sales and acquisitions, the group's CEO said on Tuesday.

"The losses in net sales resulting from divestments -- which there will probably be more of -- will have to be offset with something better suited to the (product) portfolio," CEO Jarmo Rytilahti told a news conference on Asko's 1996 results.
Asko reported 1996 profits after financial items up 26 percent on 1995, to 401 million markka from 318 million, and net sales up five percent to 7.4 billion markka.
"The best result in Asko's history," Rytilahti called it, and said the company's result this year would be "at least as good" as in 1995.
But after divestments of operations worth 316 million markka in 1996, Asko would need to acquire new operations to grow, Rytilahti said.
"Our divestments have taken away from our earnings and have taken away about a billion markka from our net sales," he said.

"There are several gold fish that we've been fishing for, but that are not in the net yet," Rytilahti said declining to say what acquisitions Asko was eying but adding that the growth would mainly be sought in its Uponor plastic pipes unit.
"The main growth will be sought in Uponor. That has been our strategy for the past three or four years," he said.

"I would hope we could find a really good acquisition for Uponor that would suit our strategy," Rytilahti said, adding that Asko had had several offers from prospective sellers of business operations, but that it was a seller's market.
With net sales of 3.8 billion markka, Uponor accounted for a good half of Asko group net sales in 1996.
Asko is aiming for organic growth of eight to 10 percent a year, Rytilahti said.
"We should achieve our organic growth target, and we should also acquire a few billion markka more in net sales over a three to five year perspective," Rytilahti said.
